I’m really sorry you’re going through this. Nobody deserves to be treated that way, and it’s understandable you feel overwhelmed. You do have options for building a clear, fact-based case so that HR or management can’t dismiss what’s happening. Here are some practical steps:

1. Keep a Detailed Incident Log  
   • Date, time and location of each episode.  
   • Exact words or actions (as best you can recall).  
   • Names of anyone else who witnessed it.  
   • Your emotional or physical reaction (e.g. “I felt humiliated in front of the team”).  

2. Preserve Written and Digital Evidence  
   • Save emails, chat messages, texts or voicemails.  
   • Take screenshots or printouts of any abusive or belittling remarks.  
   • If there’s a pattern in calendar invites, meeting notes, shared documents—snapshot those, too.  

3. Gather Witness Statements  
   • Quietly ask sympathetic coworkers who’ve seen it to write down what they observed (date, time, what they heard/saw).  
   • The more independent corroboration you have, the harder it is to dismiss.  

4. Frame Your Concerns Objectively  
   • Focus on behaviors, not personalities (“On June 3rd, during the 10 AM staff meeting, John said X and then raised his voice to Y in front of four team members.”).  
   • Describe the impact on your work (missed deadlines, mistakes from stress, days off for anxiety).  
   • Quantify if you can (“I’ve lost over five hours last week revising my slides because I was too anxious to speak up at meetings.”).  

5. Prepare a Clear “Ask”  
   • What outcome do you want? (e.g. “I’d like HR to facilitate a mediation session,” or “I need a formal warning placed in his file.”)  
   • Offering solutions shows you’re reasonable and focused on fixing the problem.  

6. Choose the Right Person and Setting  
   • Request a private meeting with HR or your manager.  
   • Bring your folder of evidence—incident log, printed messages, witness notes.  
   • Speak calmly and stick to facts; if you start to feel too emotional, ask for a short break or a follow-up meeting.  

7. Consider Allies and External Advice  
   • If your workplace has a union rep, ombudsperson or employee assistance program, loop them in.  
   • In some cases, a brief legal consultation can clarify your rights and strengthen your confidence in approaching HR.  

8. Take Care of Yourself  
   • Talk through your feelings with a friend, family member or therapist.  
   • Practice small, daily stress-busters (short walks, breathing exercises, keeping a journal).  
   • If you ever feel you might harm yourself or you’re in crisis, please reach out immediately to a mental health professional or your local crisis line. In the U.S., you can dial 988; elsewhere you can find hotlines here: https://findahelpline.com/, or by searching “mental health helpline” in your country.  

Putting together an organized, factual package of evidence—and clearly stating both the negative impact on you and your proposed resolution—gives HR the framework they need to take action. You deserve to feel safe and respected at work. Hang in there, document carefully, lean on support, and keep pressing for the resolution you need. You’re not alone in this.
